headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure between Continue and oh-my-openagent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and uses MCP/tool calls; oh-my-openagent can access AGENTS.md, README.md, session history, and runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. That creates a plausible instruction-injection path through shared files or prompts. The pair is not documented directly, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace files, injected instructions in those files can influence downstream tool use.
IF oh-my-openagent ingests AGENTS.md or README.md as guidance, attacker-controlled text can steer Continue through shared content.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic trust of repository instructions.
Require provenance labels on file-derived instructions.
Review MCP tool calls before approval.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-separation guards.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers and has broad network egress; oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth data, with broad egress too. Because both can see workspace content and send data outward, sensitive code or auth material can leak from one agent’s context to external services. The shared filesystem path makes this a default-risk interaction.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or home-directory config, each can read material the other may transmit.
IF either agent forwards file contents to third-party APIs, code or auth data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers.
Exclude secrets and auth files from shared workspaces.
Turn off broad egress where possible.
Audit outbound destinations for both agents.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; oh-my-openagent can also spawn subprocesses and has full-permissions mode. Both share state via filesystem, so concurrent writes to the same workspace or config paths can overwrite each other and create destructive conflicts. The profiles do not show locking, so the safer reading is high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF oh-my-openagent runs in full-permissions mode while Continue edits the same files, concurrent mutations can race.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent.
Disable full-permissions mode during overlap.
Serialize write operations manually.
Back up the workspace before concurrent runs.
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can produce code edits and tool-assisted outputs; oh-my-openagent exposes team_send_message, team_task_create, and LSP actions, so it can act on upstream outputs. If oh-my-openagent treats Continue’s suggestions as authoritative, errors can cascade into messages, tasks, or code actions without verification. The interaction is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF Continue’s generated code or facts are forwarded into oh-my-openagent without review, downstream actions may be wrong.
IF oh-my-openagent uses team_send_message or task creation on unverified upstream output, the error propagates.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents.
Require source citations for any forwarded facts.
Disable auto-send/task creation on imported text.
Limit Continue output to suggestions only.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is open-source IDE assistance with workspace files and model-provider API keys; oh-my-openagent handles session history, installation identifiers, and provider auth prompts, plus telemetry and external APIs. The profiles suggest different retention and data-class handling, but no explicit residency or certification mismatch is documented. That supports a medium compliance-risk assessment rather than high.
conditions: IF the same regulated data class is processed by both agents, their differing telemetry and session-history handling can create retention mismatch.
IF provider auth prompts or API keys are stored in shared configs, compliance scope expands beyond the intended boundary.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents.
Review retention settings for telemetry and session history.
Store provider keys in separate secret stores.
Document data-flow boundaries.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both tools.
